newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street balks at talk Clinton eyeing Bergsten.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street balks at talk Clinton eyeing Bergsten.

text.p: Wall Street recoiled at talk that dollar bear Fred Bergsten might garner a top spot in the second Clinton Administration.
Journal of Commerce reported Thursday that economist Bergsten, head of the Institute of International Economics, was being considered to replace Laura Tyson to head the National Economic Council.
A Bergsten appointment would be a "complete and utter disaster," said Michael Perelstein, portfolio manager of MainStay International Funds.

"It would be a terrible problem for U.S. financial markets if we brought in a person whose reputation has been to discourage foreigners from investing in U.S. securities and to bash the U.S. dollar," Perelstein said.
The newspaper noted Bergsten could suit other cabinet-level postings such as U.S. trade representative or Deputy Treasury Secretary if Lawrence Summers left that job.
Bergsten's office in Washington declined comment.
The private economist served in Treasury under President Jimmy Carter.
Bergsten has been an informal but influential adviser to Bill Clinton since his first presidential campaign. Yet some analysts doubted Clinton would consider Bergsten for such a post.

"There is very little chance that Bergsten would be considered for such a role because because he's a very independent policy maker," said John Rothfield, an international economist at Nationsbanc-CRT. "He wouldn't fit into an overall Administration policy."
The implication would be the Administration embraces Bergsten's strong view on the dollar, Rothfield added.
Under Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, the White House has steadfastly touted the virtues of a strong dollar.
The U.S. currency plunged to a post World War II low of 79.75 yen April 19, 1995, but had rebounded nearly 40 percent to trade around 111.32 yen by Thursday afternoon dealings.
Dollar bear Bergsten, by constrast, predicted in October the U.S. unit would weaken next year and end 1997 at 100 yen.

Furthermore, in a recent article in "The Economist," Bergsten wrote that with the yen hovering around 115 to the dollar, action is urgently needed to halt the depreciation of the yen and reverse it "at least modestly."
It is Bergsten's bearish dollar views that rankle investors.
"What's not understood is that the dollar today is an extremely important linchpin in keeping (U.S.) rates where they are," Perelstein said.
He warned that if Bergsten in a cabinet post talked the dollar down, foreign investors might bale out of U.S. bonds which could lead to higher interest rates for consumers.
The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yield is hovering near 6.43 percent, its lowest since the close of March 7.
Perelstein noted that some U.S. investors, well stocked with Treasuries, are shifting away from bonds into equities.
"If we don't encourage foreign investors to take up the slack, we're going to be in deep trouble," he said.
Other market participants played down any potential influence Bergsten might exercise should he join the Clinton team.

"Were hearing that story from reputable (sources), and it's not beyond the realm of possibility," said Tom Arnold, chief currency dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York, referring to the Bergsten reports. "But is he going to go in and change (Group of Seven) currency policy? That's highly doubtful."
